newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: West scrambles to defuse Serbia crisis.
newsitem.headline: West scrambles to defuse Serbia crisis.

text.p: The international community intensified efforts on Saturday to help end the month-old crisis between Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and opposition parties which accuse him of election fraud.

Belgrade students staged their biggest demonstration in weeks on Saturday, with reporters estimating up to 40,000 protestors marching through the streets cheered by Belgraders lining the pavement or on windows and balconies.

Hours later tens of thousands of opposition supporters, waving flags, blowing thrumpets and whistles and accompanied by several gipsy bands, started their daily march and organisers said they hoped to beat Friday's record of 200,000.

Serbia's opposition and students have mounted more than three weeks of peaceful street protests since the Zajedno opposition coalition claimed Milosevic's ruling socialists cheated it of victory in biggest Serbian cities, including Belgrade, during November local elections.

At their Dublin summit, European Union leaders set conditions for an international team to verify the regularity of last month's polls, including the right to re-run them under inernational supervision, mediator Carl Bildt said on Saturday.

Under pressure from daily mass street protests, Milosevic offered on Friday to allow the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to send a delegation to check the fairness of the poll.
A declaration adopted at the Dublin summit called on Yugoslavia to "demonstrate full respect for human and minority rights and the observance of democratic norms".
"The OSCE will wish to consider the conditions for such a mission, notably in relation to the right to recommend a reversal of the annulments or a rerun of some elections," the EU draft said.
The United States on Friday branded Milosevic's offer a whitewash, but the Europeans were more inclined to use it as a potential lever for a democratic transition in Belgrade.
Bildt called Milosevic to commit himself to allow media freedom and begin a dialogue with the oppsotion.

"We have no interest whatsoever in an economic and social collapse of Serbia," Bildt said, but he added: "There is no way that Serbia can remain an enclave (in Europe) of ideas that normally end up on the scrap heap of history."
Bildt said Milosevic's inability or unwillingness to reform Serbia's economy was the main cause of the current crisis.

Diplomats said there was debate among EU governments over the significance of the daily marches by up to 200,000 demonstrators in Belgrade and how can a democratic transition be achieved without triggering repression or bloodbath.
Some countries argue strong support for the Serbian opposition strong support while others urge caution, noting that workers have yet to join students and intellectuals in the protests.
Some EU diplomats were concerned that Milosevic could crack down with his widely-feared police against the demonstrations, into their 27th day on Saturday.

"These demonstrations are the biggest ever, the square in front of the Philosophy College is completely packed and adjoining streets too," independent Belgrade radio B92 reported on the student protest.

Security forces were keeping a low profile in line with Milosevic's repeated promises to the West that he would not resort to violence to squash the protests like he did in 1991, when he sent in tanks.
